section.heading: 2.3 The Limit Laws
Learning Objectives

list.item: Recognize the basic limit laws.
Use the limit laws to evaluate the limit of a function.
Evaluate the limit of a function by factoring.
Use the limit laws to evaluate the limit of a polynomial or rational function.
Evaluate the limit of a function by factoring or by using conjugates.
Evaluate the limit of a function by using the squeeze theorem.

section.paragraph: In the previous section, we evaluated limits by looking at graphs or by constructing a table of values. In this section, we establish laws for calculating limits and learn how to apply these laws. In the Student Project at the end of this section, you have the opportunity to apply these limit laws to derive the formula for the area of a circle by adapting a method devised by the Greek mathematician Archimedes. We begin by restating two useful limit results from the previous section. These two results, together with the limit laws, serve as a foundation for calculating many limits.
section.heading: Evaluating Limits with the Limit Laws
section.paragraph: The first two limit laws were stated in Two Important Limits and we repeat them here. These basic results, together with the other limit laws, allow us to evaluate limits of many algebraic functions.

note.title: Basic Limit Results
note.heading: Basic Limit Results
note.paragraph: For any real number a and any constant c,

list.item: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }x = a$$ (2.14)
$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }c = c$$ (2.15)

problem.paragraph: Evaluate each of the following limits using Basic Limit Results.

list.item: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x$$
$$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }5$$
The limit of x as x approaches a is a: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x = 2.$$

section.paragraph: We now take a look at the limit laws, the individual properties of limits. The proofs that these laws hold are omitted here.

note.title: Limit Laws
note.heading: Limit Laws
note.paragraph: Let $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ over some open interval containing a. Assume that L and M are real numbers such that $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = M.$$ Let c be a constant. Then, each of the following statements holds:
Sum law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x) + g(x)} \right) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) + \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L + M$$
Difference law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x) - g(x)} \right) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) - \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L - M$$
Constant multiple law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }cf(x) = c \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = cL$$
Product law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x) \cdot g(x)} \right) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L \cdot M$$
Quotient law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)}{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x)} = \frac{L}{M}$$ for $$M \neq 0$$
Power law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x)} \right)^{n} = \left( {\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)} \right)^{n} = L^{n}$$ for every positive integer n.

Root law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\sqrt[n]{f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{L}$$ for all L if n is odd and for $$L \geq 0$$ if n is even and $$f(x) \geq 0$$ .

section.paragraph: We now practice applying these limit laws to evaluate a limit.

example.title: Evaluating a Limit Using Limit Laws

problem.paragraph: Use the limit laws to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }\left( {4x + 2} \right).$$

solution.paragraph: Let’s apply the limit laws one step at a time to be sure we understand how they work. We need to keep in mind the requirement that, at each application of a limit law, the new limits must exist for the limit law to be applied.

$$\begin{array}{clccl} {\underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }\left( {4x + 2} \right)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }4x + \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }2} & & & \text{Apply the sum law.} \\ & {= 4 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }x + \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }2} & & & \text{Apply the constant multiple law.} \\ & {= 4 \cdot (-3) + 2 = -10.} & & & \text{Apply the basic limit results and simplify.} \end{array}$$

problem.paragraph: Use the limit laws to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{2x^{2} - 3x + 1}{x^{3} + 4}.$$

solution.paragraph: To find this limit, we need to apply the limit laws several times. Again, we need to keep in mind that as we rewrite the limit in terms of other limits, each new limit must exist for the limit law to be applied.

$$\begin{array}{clccl} & & & & \\ & & & & \\ {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{2x^{2} - 3x + 1}{x^{3} + 4}} & {= \frac{\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\left( {2x^{2} - 3x + 1} \right)}{\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\left( {x^{3} + 4} \right)}} & & & { \text{Apply the quotient law, making sure that.} (2)^{3} + 4 \neq 0} \\ & {= \frac{2 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{2} - 3 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }1}{\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{3} + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }4}} & & & \text{Apply the sum law and constant multiple law.} \\ & {= \frac{2 \cdot \left( {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x} \right)^{2} - 3 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }1}{\left( {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x} \right)^{3} + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }4}} & & & \text{Apply the power law.} \\ & {= \frac{2(4) - 3(2) + 1}{(2)^{3} + 4} = \frac{1}{4}.} & & & \text{Apply the basic limit laws and simplify.} \end{array}$$

problem.paragraph: Use the limit laws to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 6}{\lim }\left( {2x - 1} \right)\sqrt{x + 4}.$$ In each step, indicate the limit law applied.

section.heading: Limits of Polynomial and Rational Functions
section.paragraph: By now you have probably noticed that, in each of the previous examples, it has been the case that $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = f(a).$$ This is not always true, but it does hold for all polynomials for any choice of a and for all rational functions at all values of a for which the rational function is defined.

note.title: Limits of Polynomial and Rational Functions
note.heading: Limits of Polynomial and Rational Functions
note.paragraph: Let $$p(x)$$ and $$q(x)$$ be polynomial functions. Let a be a real number. Then,
$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }p(x) = p(a)$$
$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \frac{p(a)}{q(a)} \text{when} q(a) \neq 0.$$

section.paragraph: To see that this theorem holds, consider the polynomial $$p(x) = c_{n}x^{n} + c_{n - 1}x^{n - 1} + \cdots + c_{1}x + c_{0}.$$ By applying the sum, constant multiple, and power laws, we end up with

$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }p(x)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {c_{n}x^{n} + c_{n - 1}x^{n - 1} + \cdots + c_{1}x + c_{0}} \right)} \\ & {= c_{n}\left( {\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }x} \right)^{n} + c_{n - 1}\left( {\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }x} \right)^{n - 1} + \cdots + c_{1}\left( {\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }x} \right) + \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }c_{0}} \\ & {= c_{n}a^{n} + c_{n - 1}a^{n - 1} + \cdots + c_{1}a + c_{0}} \\ & {= p(a).} \end{array}$$
It now follows from the quotient law that if $$p(x)$$ and $$q(x)$$ are polynomials for which $$q(a) \neq 0,$$ then
$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \frac{p(a)}{q(a)}.$$
Example 2.16 applies this result.

section.heading: Additional Limit Evaluation Techniques
section.paragraph: As we have seen, we may evaluate easily the limits of polynomials and limits of some (but not all) rational functions by direct substitution. However, as we saw in the introductory section on limits, it is certainly possible for $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$ to exist when $$f(a)$$ is undefined. The following observation allows us to evaluate many limits of this type:
If for all $$x \neq a,f(x) = g(x)$$ over some open interval containing a, then $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x).$$
To understand this idea better, consider the limit $$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}.$$
The function
$$\begin{array}{cl} {f(x)} & {= \frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}} \\ & {= \frac{\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}{x - 1}} \end{array}$$
and the function $$g(x) = x + 1$$ are identical for all values of $$x \neq 1.$$ The graphs of these two functions are shown in Figure 2.24.

image.alt: Two graphs side by side. The first is a graph of g(x) = x + 1, a linear function with y intercept at (0,1) and x intercept at (-1,0). The second is a graph of f(x) = (x^2 – 1) / (x – 1). This graph is identical to the first for all x not equal to 1, as there is an open circle at (1,2) in the second graph.

figure.caption: The graphs of $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ are identical for all $$x \neq 1.$$ Their limits at 1 are equal.

section.paragraph: We see that

$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}{x - 1}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\left( {x + 1} \right)} \\ & {= 2.} \end{array}$$

The limit has the form $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)},$$ where $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = 0$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = 0.$$ (In this case, we say that $${f(x)}/{g(x)}$$ has the indeterminate form $${0/0} \text{.)}$$ The following Problem-Solving Strategy provides a general outline for evaluating limits of this type.

note.title: Problem-Solving Strategy
note.heading: Calculating a Limit When $$f(x)/g(x)$$ has the Indeterminate Form 0/0

list.item: First, we need to make sure that our function has the appropriate form and cannot be evaluated immediately using the limit laws.

We then need to find a function that is equal to $$h(x) = {{f(x)}/{g(x)}}$$ for all $$x \neq a$$ over some interval containing a. To do this, we may need to try one or more of the following steps: If $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ are polynomials, we should factor each function and cancel out any common factors. If the numerator or denominator contains a difference involving a square root, we should try multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the expression involving the square root. If $${f(x)}/{g(x)}$$ is a complex fraction, we begin by simplifying it.
Last, we apply the limit laws.

section.paragraph: Let’s now revisit one-sided limits. Simple modifications in the limit laws allow us to apply them to one-sided limits. For example, to apply the limit laws to a limit of the form $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }h(x),$$ we require the function $$h(x)$$ to be defined over an open interval of the form $$\left( {b,a} \right);$$ for a limit of the form $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }h(x),$$ we require the function $$h(x)$$ to be defined over an open interval of the form $$\left( {a,c} \right).$$ Example 2.21 illustrates this point.

example.title: Evaluating a One-Sided Limit Using the Limit Laws

problem.paragraph: Evaluate each of the following limits, if possible.

list.item: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}$$
$$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}$$

solution.paragraph: Figure 2.25 illustrates the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ and aids in our understanding of these limits.

image.alt: A graph of the function f(x) = sqrt(x-3). Visually, the function looks like the top half of a parabola opening to the right with vertex at (3,0).

list.item: The function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ is defined over the interval $$\left\lbrack {3,+\infty} \right).$$ Since this function is not defined to the left of 3, we cannot apply the limit laws to compute $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}.$$ In fact, since $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ is undefined to the left of 3, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}$$ does not exist.

Since $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ is defined to the right of 3, the limit laws do apply to $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}.$$ By applying these limit laws we obtain $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3} = 0.$$

section.heading: The Squeeze Theorem
section.paragraph: The techniques we have developed thus far work very well for algebraic functions, but we are still unable to evaluate limits of very basic trigonometric functions. The next theorem, called the squeeze theorem, proves very useful for establishing basic trigonometric limits. This theorem allows us to calculate limits by “squeezing” a function, with a limit at a point a that is unknown, between two functions having a common known limit at a. Figure 2.27 illustrates this idea.

image.alt: A graph of three functions over a small interval. All three functions curve. Over this interval, the function g(x) is trapped between the functions h(x), which gives greater y values for the same x values, and f(x), which gives smaller y values for the same x values. The functions all approach the same limit when x=a.

figure.caption: The Squeeze Theorem applies when $$f(x) \leq g(x) \leq h(x)$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }h(x).$$

note.title: The Squeeze Theorem
note.heading: The Squeeze Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$f(x),g(x),$$ and $$h(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ over an open interval containing a. If
$$f(x) \leq g(x) \leq h(x)$$
for all $$x \neq a$$ in an open interval containing a and
$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }h(x)$$
where L is a real number, then $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L.$$

problem.paragraph: Apply the squeeze theorem to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }x\cos x.$$

solution.paragraph: Because $$-1 \leq \cos x \leq 1$$ for all x, we have $$\left. - \middle| x \middle| \leq x\cos x \leq \middle| x \right|$$ . Since $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( \left. - \middle| x \right| \right) = 0 = \underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }|x|,$$ from the squeeze theorem, we obtain $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }x\cos x = 0.$$ The graphs of $$\left. f(x) = - \middle| x \middle| ,g(x) = x\cos x, \right.$$ and $$\left. h(x) = \middle| x \right|$$ are shown in Figure 2.28.

image.alt: The graph of three functions: h(x) = x, f(x) = -x, and g(x) = xcos(x). The first, h(x) = x, is a linear function with slope of 1 going through the origin. The second, f(x), is also a linear function with slope of −1; going through the origin. The third, g(x) = xcos(x), curves between the two and goes through the origin. It opens upward for x>0 and downward for x>0.

figure.caption: The graphs of $$f(x),g(x),$$ and $$h(x)$$ are shown around the point $$x = 0.$$

problem.paragraph: Use the squeeze theorem to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }x^{2}\sin \frac{1}{x}.$$

section.paragraph: We now use the squeeze theorem to tackle several very important limits. Although this discussion is somewhat lengthy, these limits prove invaluable for the development of the material in both the next section and the next chapter. The first of these limits is $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\sin \theta.$$ Consider the unit circle shown in Figure 2.29. In the figure, we see that $$\sin \theta$$ is the y-coordinate on the unit circle and it corresponds to the line segment shown in blue. The radian measure of angle θ is the length of the arc it subtends on the unit circle. Therefore, we see that for $$0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2},0 < \sin \theta < \theta.$$

image.alt: A diagram of the unit circle in the x,y plane – it is a circle with radius 1 and center at the origin. A specific point (cos(theta), sin(theta)) is labeled in quadrant 1 on the edge of the circle. This point is one vertex of a right triangle inside the circle, with other vertices at the origin and (cos(theta), 0). As such, the lengths of the sides are cos(theta) for the base and sin(theta) for the height, where theta is the angle created by the hypotenuse and base. The radian measure of angle theta is the length of the arc it subtends on the unit circle. The diagram shows that for 0 < theta < pi/2, 0 < sin(theta) < theta.

figure.caption: The sine function is shown as a line on the unit circle.

section.paragraph: Because $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }0 = 0$$ and $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\theta = 0,$$ by using the squeeze theorem we conclude that
$$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\sin \theta = 0.$$

To see that $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\sin \theta = 0$$ as well, observe that for $$- \frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < 0,0 < -\theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$$ and hence, $$0 < \sin \left( {- \theta} \right) < -\theta.$$ Consequently, $$0 < - \sin \theta < -\theta.$$ It follows that $$0 > \sin \theta > \theta.$$ An application of the squeeze theorem produces the desired limit. Thus, since $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\sin \theta = 0$$ and $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\sin \theta = 0,$$
$$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\sin \theta = 0.$$
Next, using the identity $$\cos \theta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\theta}$$ for $$- \frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2},$$ we see that
$$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\cos \theta = \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\theta} = 1.$$

We now take a look at a limit that plays an important role in later chapters—namely, $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sin \theta}{\theta}.$$ To evaluate this limit, we use the unit circle in Figure 2.30. Notice that this figure adds one additional triangle to Figure 2.30. We see that the length of the side opposite angle θ in this new triangle is $$\tan \theta.$$ Thus, we see that for $$0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2},\sin \theta < \theta < \tan \theta.$$

image.alt: The same diagram as the previous one. However, the triangle is expanded. The base is now from the origin to (1,0). The height goes from (1,0) to (1, tan(theta)). The hypotenuse goes from the origin to (1, tan(theta)). As such, the height is now tan(theta). It shows that for 0 < theta < pi/2, sin(theta) < theta < tan(theta).

figure.caption: The sine and tangent functions are shown as lines on the unit circle.

section.paragraph: By dividing by $$\sin \theta$$ in all parts of the inequality, we obtain
$$1 < \frac{\theta}{\sin \theta} < \frac{1}{\cos \theta}.$$
Equivalently, we have
$$1 > \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} > \cos \theta.$$

Since $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }1 = 1 = \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\cos \theta,$$ we conclude that $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.$$ By applying a manipulation similar to that used in demonstrating that $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\sin \theta = 0,$$ we can show that $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.$$ Thus,
$$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.$$
In Example 2.25 we use this limit to establish $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta} = 0.$$ This limit also proves useful in later chapters.

note.title: Student Project
note.heading: Deriving the Formula for the Area of a Circle
note.paragraph: Some of the geometric formulas we take for granted today were first derived by methods that anticipate some of the methods of calculus. The Greek mathematician Archimedes (ca. 287−212; BCE) was particularly inventive, using polygons inscribed within circles to approximate the area of the circle as the number of sides of the polygon increased. He never came up with the idea of a limit, but we can use this idea to see what his geometric constructions could have predicted about the limit.

We can estimate the area of a circle by computing the area of an inscribed regular polygon. Think of the regular polygon as being made up of n triangles. By taking the limit as the vertex angle of these triangles goes to zero, you can obtain the area of the circle. To see this, carry out the following steps:

If an n-sided regular polygon is inscribed in a circle of radius r, find a relationship between θ and n. Solve this for n. Keep in mind there are 2π radians in a circle. (Use radians, not degrees.)
Find an expression for the area of the n-sided polygon in terms of r and θ.

To find a formula for the area of the circle, find the limit of the expression in step 4 as θ goes to zero. (Hint: $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {\sin \theta} \right)}{\theta} = 1 \text{).}$$

note.paragraph: The technique of estimating areas of regions by using polygons is revisited in Introduction to Integration.
